stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: An agronomist wanted to estimate the mean wheat yield, in bushels per acre, for all wheat farms in a state. The agronomist randomly selected 40 farms from the membership list of the state's Irrigated Grain Growers Cooperative, which accepts only farms that irrigate their fields. The mean yield of the selected farms was 72 bushels per acre.
choices: Because the farms were chosen at random, 72 bushels per acre is a sound estimate for all wheat farms in the state.
The only problem is size; randomly choosing 400 cooperative farms would give a sound estimate for the whole state.
The farms were chosen at random from irrigated farms only, so the estimate may be biased for all farms in the state.
Randomly choosing 40 farms that do not irrigate would give a sound estimate of the mean yield for the whole state.
explanation: The agronomist wants to know about all wheat farms in the state. The farms were chosen at random, but only from a cooperative that accepts irrigated farms. Random selection lets you generalize only to the group you selected from, which here is irrigated cooperative farms. Irrigated farms may yield more than farms that rely on rain, so the estimate may be biased for the state as a whole.

A.why: You saw the word 'random' and stopped there. The farms were chosen at random from irrigated cooperative farms only, so the result can't be stretched to every wheat farm in the state.

B.why: You blamed the sample size. Choosing 400 farms from the same irrigated-only list still leaves out every farm that doesn't irrigate, so the bias stays.

D.why: You swapped one subgroup for its opposite. Farms that don't irrigate are no more representative of all farms than irrigated farms are.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A folklore student wanted to estimate the percentage of adults in the town of Marrow Bend who believe the legend of the Lantern Woman, a ghost said to walk the old mill road. The student set up a table at the town's yearly Lantern Night parade, which is held in honor of the legend, and asked 200 adults who stopped at the table. Of these adults, 150 said they believe the legend.
choices: Since 150 of the 200 adults believe the legend, about 75% of the adults in Marrow Bend believe it as well.
Parade-goers who stop at a table about the legend are not a random sample of town adults, so the result may be biased.
The sample of 200 is too small; asking 2,000 adults at the next Lantern Night parade would give an accurate estimate.
Asking 200 adults who stayed home during Lantern Night would give an accurate estimate for all adults in the town.
explanation: The student wants to know about all adults in Marrow Bend but only asked people who came to a parade celebrating the legend and chose to stop at the table. Those people are probably more interested in the legend, and more likely to believe it, than adults in general. The sample wasn't randomly chosen from the town, so the result may be biased.

A.why: You worked out 150 ÷ 200 = 75% correctly and then applied it to the whole town. A large majority in a self-selected group of festival-goers doesn't tell you about everyone else.

C.why: You blamed the sample size. Asking 2,000 people at the same parade repeats the same selection problem on a larger scale.

D.why: You swapped one unrepresentative group for its opposite. Adults who stayed home that night are not a random sample of the town either.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A city's public works department wanted to learn how all drivers in the city rate the condition of city streets. The department posted a rating form inside a smartphone app that residents use to report potholes. Of the 480 app users who chose to fill out the form, 360 rated the condition of city streets as poor.
choices: Because 360 of the 480 respondents chose poor, about three-fourths of all drivers in the city rate the streets as poor.
With 480 responses the method is sound, but a larger number of responses is needed before drawing any conclusion.
Sending the form to 480 randomly chosen app users would give a reliable estimate of how all city drivers rate streets.
Respondents chose to answer and use an app for reporting potholes, so the results may not represent all city drivers.
explanation: The population is all drivers in the city. The respondents, though, used a pothole-reporting app and also chose to answer, so they were selected twice over. People who report potholes are likely to be the ones most bothered by bad streets. A sample like that isn't random or representative, so the results may be biased.

C.why: You fixed the self-selection but kept the wrong sampling frame. A random sample of pothole-app users lets you generalize only to app users, not to all drivers in the city.

choices: Owners who called to report well problems likely had worse-affected wells, so 80% may overstate the county percentage.

choices: Because the 80 tiles were chosen at random, about 25% of all tiles the factory made last year would crack under the test.
